transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-11
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ollie Park (Redwood SE), Janelle Ruiz (Redwood SE observer); Diego Rojas, Emily Stone, Nikhil Patel, Asha Menon (Stratosphere)
Links shared: demo deck (https://redwood.app/decks/stratosphere-demo), SOC2 & security docs (https://redwood.app/security/soc2), benchmark sheet (https://sheets.google.com/benchmark-sample)

Summary:
Quick hands-on walkthrough of Redwood JSON-mode (schema-first) + function/tool calling flow; show Console config, Optimize recommendations, and how guardrails & fallbacks work across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private VPC. Goal: align on pilot scope, perf expectations, and security checklist.

Topics covered:
- JSON mode and schema validation in runtime
- Tool/function calling with typed responses and safe fallbacks
- Console: route config, rollout and tracing
- Redwood Optimize recommendations (batching, quantization profiles)
- Private deployment considerations: VPC, KMS, SSO, audit logs
- Pilot scope and success criteria (latency, token cost, quality)

Action items (also in metadata):
- Send pricing and SKUs for dedicated pools
- Run quick perf sketch for 2k token baseline
- Customer to provide prompt set + token stats
- Customer to provide security requirements

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll give a focused demo of our schema-first JSON mode and how that ties into tool calling and the console. Quick intros?
[00:18] Diego (Stratosphere): Hi, Diego here. Head of Platform. We're trying to replace an internal inference glue layer and want safer outputs and predictable costs.
[00:25] Emily (Stratosphere): Emily, ML eng, working on prompt templates and evals.
[00:28] Nikhil (Stratosphere): Nikhil, security architect. I'll cover compliance bits.
[00:33] Maya: Great. Ollie from our SE team will drive the live part.
[00:38] Ollie (Redwood): Alright, jumping in — first slide is our JSON mode. The idea: you give a schema for the response, the model is constrained to that schema and the runtime validates, applies typed-tool calls if needed, and there's a fallback orchestration when parse fails.
[00:54] Emily: When you say "constrained" do you mean strict validation? Like if the model returns a stray field it fails?
[01:02] Ollie: Good question. By default the runtime will validate against the JSON schema. If it fails parse we can do a couple patterns: 1) auto-repair heuristics (best-effort), 2) call a small correction model and re-run, or 3) fall back to a looser schema and still surface structured fields. You can choose policy per-route in Console.
[01:30] Diego: That last bit — policy per-route — we need that for billing and risk. We want strict on payments but more tolerant for exploratory agent tooling.
[01:39] Ollie: Exactly, route policy + rollout. In Console you can set schema-strictness, fallback targets, and then rollout to a percent of traffic.
[01:49] Maya: I'll show the console after the quick demo so you can see the config.
[01:55] Ollie: Live demo — I'll call the API with a schema that expects an array of address objects and a tool call to an internal geocode service. Note: the tool-calling handshake is JSON-first, so the model returns a typed object that triggers an HTTP tool.
[02:12] [00:02:12] Ollie: (typing) sending request... the response comes back — neat, we get a typed invocation: {"tool":"geocode","args":{"address":"123 Rainier Ave"}} then the runtime invokes the geocode tool and patches the original JSON with coordinates.
[02:33] Emily: Is the tool invocation synchronous? We have some tools that take 700-800 ms, others are faster.
[02:39] Ollie: By default it's sync, but the runtime supports async hooks and background enrichment. For user-facing latency paths we recommend small helper services or cached KV lookups.
[02:52] Nikhil: How does caching interact with PII? We can't keep raw addresses in an open cache.
[02:59] Ollie: Good flag — in Console you can set cache policies per-route; the platform supports encrypted prefix caching and redaction before storage. For Private deployments you can configure KMS/HSM for cache encryption keys.
[03:12] Maya: This is where Optimize comes in. It surfaces caching suggestions (prefixes that hit often), batching windows, and quantization profiles that keep quality.
[03:21] Diego: Tell us more about Optimize's recommendations — we have bursty traffic and don't want to over-batch.
[03:27] Ollie: Optimize looks at your token distribution and latency SLOs. For low-latency routes it suggests micro-batching plus KV caching; for throughput-heavy jobs it suggests larger batching and a different quant profile. We'll show a sample recommendation against your uploaded prompt stats.
[03:44] [00:03:44] Ollie: Switching to Console — here is the route config: the schema is attached, validation mode set to 'strict-with-correction', fallback target is a smaller model variant and a canary. You can also enable tracing to link tokens to spans in your app.
[04:03] Emily: The 'strict-with-correction' — is that the auto repair you mentioned?
[04:08] Ollie: Yes, small repair attempt via a micro-model step; if that fails, it falls back to designated target (e.g., smaller model or human review).
[04:16] Asha (Stratosphere): From a product POV we need deterministic webhooks for external services. If the model sometimes calls the tool and sometimes not, can we get consistent events?
[04:26] Maya: You can enforce deterministic tool invocation by schema constraints (required fields and explicit tool trigger signals). If you need absolute determinism, we suggest deterministic validation rules combined with a transaction log/audit trail — Console exposes an audit stream.
[04:40] Nikhil: Audit stream — is that sufficient for compliance? We need immutable logs for actions and SSO events.
[04:47] Maya: For Hosted we provide audit logs with retention tiers; for Dedicated/Private you can ship logs to your SIEM and enable WORM retention and HSM-backed signing. We'll share a compliance playbook.
[04:58] Diego: Regarding deployment modes — we want predictable latency for a customer-facing feature. Which mode do customers typically pick?
[05:05] Ollie: Many start Hosted for speed to production, then move to Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) when they need predictable throughput. Regulated customers pick Private (VPC/on-prem) for data residency and KMS control.
[05:17] Emily: For the pilot we'd like deterministic latency numbers at the p50/p95 for our 2k token prompts.
[05:23] Ollie: We'll run a targeted benchmark. For context, Optimize will recommend batch size, target model (quant profile), and expected token/s. We'll include p50/p95 estimates from the perf sketch.
[05:34] [00:05:34] Emily: Another thing — our current internal stack strips some json fields occasionally when the model over-generates. How do you handle stray fields in typed responses?
[05:44] Ollie: Runtime validation will either reject the response or sanitize it depending on the policy. There's also a 'field allowlist' and 'scrub unknowns' flag. For safety we usually recommend scrub unknowns = true and surface the discrepant payload in the audit log.
[06:00] Maya: We also have runtime guardrails for tool side effects: a dry-run mode so tools can be validated before they perform writes, and a policy engine for rate-limiting tool calls.
[06:10] Diego: That dry-run would help our QA flow. Can we replay the audit events to reproduce a call?
[06:15] Janelle (Redwood): Yes — Console allows replay of recorded sessions to a sandbox. We also provide linkable traces and a replay token that maps to the input prompt and model decisions.
[06:25] Nikhil: For keys and encryption: do you support customer-managed keys?
[06:29] Maya: Yes — for Private/Dedicated you can bring your own KMS/HSM; for Hosted we offer KMS integration and a BYOK path for enterprise customers.
[06:38] Nikhil: What about SOC 2 and ISO evidence?
[06:41] Maya: We'll send our SOC2 report and the compliance artifact pack. (link shared earlier).
[06:47] [00:06:47] Diego: Ok let's talk failure modes: what happens when the model halluc doesn’t conform to schema mid-stream — e.g., partial arrays or truncated responses?
[06:58] Ollie: Two important behaviors. Streaming paths: we validate on flush points and can close stream with a structured error payload if violation detected; non-streaming: we run post-response validation and either auto-repair or route to fallback. For partial arrays we have a 'partial-accept' flag so downstream can handle incremental patches.
[07:19] Emily: And latency when repair happens? That could be bad for UX.
[07:22] Ollie: Repair loops add a small overhead — Optimize will show expected cost/latency impact for repair heuristics. Recommendation: prefer lightweight micro-repair, and for heavier corrections route to background enrichment.
[07:34] Asha: Let's cover the pilot scope and success criteria. Diego?
[07:38] Diego: Pilot scope: 1) Integrate 2 routes with JSON-mode schemas, 2) include a geocode tool invocation flow, 3) run benchmarks for 2k token path, 4) verify audit and SSO flows. Success: p95 < 800ms for user-facing route, cost per 1k tokens within X% of current infra, and zero schema-driven production errors in the 2-week window.
[08:02] Maya: Good. We'll propose a 2-week pilot with a 1-week calibration period and a 1-week production-like window.
[08:09] Diego: Sounds fair. What's needed from us?
[08:12] Ollie: Sample prompts, expected traffic distribution, and access to a staging tool endpoint for the geocode service.
[08:18] Emily: We'll produce a prompt set and upload to the benchmark sheet.
[08:22] Nikhil: We'll send SSO metadata and KMS policy.
[08:25] Maya: Great. Now quick deep dive on Optimize recommendations — I'll show a few examples where we trimmed cost by 30% using prefix caching + quant profile change.
[08:36] Ollie: Example: for high prefix reuse we suggested an LRU prefix cache with encrypted keys and micro-batching at 30ms window; saved tokens by avoiding repeated context.
[08:49] Emily: That LRU caching — is it per-customer or shared?
[08:53] Ollie: Per-customer namespace. In Hosted it's logically isolated; in Dedicated/Private it's physically isolated per pool and keys.
[08:59] Diego: Any limitations with SDKs? We use Node and Go.
[09:03] Janelle: We have first-class SDKs for both, and the tool-calling and schema helpers are available in the client libs. We'll send sample snippets.
[09:12] [00:09:12] Ollie: Running through a failure simulation — model returns extra field 'debug_info' and the schema disallows it. Runtime logs the event, repair attempt added a 'partial' flag, and console shows trace with the discrepant token range.
[09:33] Nikhil: For our security review, do you provide static architecture diagrams for Private deployments?
[09:38] Maya: Yes — we'll include a Private deployment architecture diagram and network flow with firewall rules for your infra team.
[09:44] Diego: About cost — what's the expected cadence to move from Hosted to Dedicated?
[09:48] Maya: Typically customers hit a throughput or SLA breakpoint; we have thresholds in Console for recommending Dedicated. We'll include commitment vs burst pricing in the pricing doc.
[09:57] Emily: For our evals we want to instrument model quality regressions — can Redwood tie eval differences to model/quantization changes?
[10:04] Ollie: Yes — we can run continuous evals on your prompt set and produce regression alerts tied to model version + quant profile. The Console UI lets you pin a baseline and receive alerts when quality drops.
[10:15] Asha: Any gotchas with long-runner tool calls and concurrency?
[10:19] Ollie: For long-running tools use async hooks and job orchestration, set separate worker pools. Runtime supports rate-limited tool queues and TTLs.
[10:27] [00:10:27] Maya: Quick pause — does anyone have outstanding security objections before we dive into config snippets?
[10:33] Nikhil: One ask: encryption-at-rest with BYOK and auditable key rotation.
[10:38] Maya: Noted — BYOK + rotation policy supported in Private/Dedicated; Hosted BYOK path available for enterprise. We'll add to action items.
[10:44] Ollie: Now Console quick config: route selector, attach schema, set 'strict-with-correction' policy, enable tracing and audit. I'll show a rollout to 10% with auto-fallback to the smaller model if p95 exceeds threshold.
[10:58] Emily: How do you measure p95 in the rollout? Is that token-level or request-level?
[11:02] Ollie: Request-level latencies that include model and tool call times. Console reports token-level breakdowns as well, including compute vs tool vs network.
[11:12] Diego: If we need on-call support during pilot, what's the SLA?
[11:16] Maya: Hosted basic support included; pilot customers typically get an elevated support path. For Dedicated we offer a higher SLA and a designated solutions engineer. We'll propose a support plan in the pricing doc.
[11:28] [00:11:28] Asha: Can we set a kill-switch for problematic tool invocations?
[11:32] Ollie: Yes. There's a per-route emergency stop and policy-based kill-switch for tool types. You can set thresholds for tool call rates that trigger automatic disable.
[11:40] Nikhil: About logging — can we redact fields before logs leave our VPC?
[11:43] Maya: For Private we can set redaction hooks and ensure logs are stored in your storage; for Hosted we offer configurable redaction rules and encrypted shipping.
[11:52] Diego: Ok conceivably we want to start with Hosted but with strict contract and then move to Dedicated.
[11:58] Maya: That's a common path — we'll mark that in next steps.
[12:02] Ollie: One more demo note — function/tool calling supports a verification token so upstream tools can validate the call came from Redwood runtime.
[12:12] Emily: That's helpful for preventing spoofing.
[12:15] [00:12:15] Maya: Quick pause — any final questions before we move to the wrap?
[12:18] Diego: Not yet. Nikhil will follow up with security specifics.
[12:21] Nikhil: We'll send an initial 2-page requirement doc.
[12:24] Maya: Perfect — recap and next steps.
[12:27] Recap: 
- Pilot: 2 routes, JSON-mode + geocode tool, 2-week window (1 week calibration, 1 week production-like)
- Deliverables from Redwood: pricing + SKUs, perf sketch, sample SDK snippets, SOC2 + Private architecture diagram, replay/audit instructions
- Deliverables from Stratosphere: prompt set + token stats, staging geocode endpoint, SSO/KMS requirements

[00:12:57] Action items (spoken):
Maya: I'll send the pricing doc, SKUs and propose pilot slots by EOD Monday (2027-06-13).
Ollie: I'll run a quick perf sketch and share numbers by Wednesday (2027-06-15).
Emily: We'll upload the prompt set and token distribution to the spreadsheet by Tuesday (2027-06-14).
Nikhil: We'll provide SSO/KMS requirements and an initial compliance doc by Tuesday (2027-06-14).

[00:13:40] Diego: OK thanks, that sounds good.
[00:13:45] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[00:13:51] (call ends)

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mishear of technical terms (e.g., 'K-V cash' instead of 'KV cache', 'quantizatin' spelled in audio notes), some crosstalk in Q+A.
